text: This chapter kicks off the capstone that runs through the rest of the course: your own small, real, honestly-scoped research project, built using every skill from the first two chapters, ending in a written report and a presentation.

This lesson covers the overall capstone structure and what gets delivered at the end, three realistic capstone project types with concrete examples, how to evaluate a candidate topic against your actual available resources and timeline, and what a capstone is not expected to be.

Across Chapters 3 through 5, you will pick and scope a project in this chapter, build the experimental setup and run it in Chapter 4, handling whatever actually happens including unexpected results, and write up and present your findings professionally in Chapter 5. The deliverables are a written report covering methods, results, limitations, and conclusions, plus a presentation suitable for both a technical and a non-specialist audience.

Three realistic project types. Reproduction plus extension: reproduce a specific, modest published result, then extend it in one well-defined direction, like a different circuit size or device. A comparative benchmark: design your own comparison that doesn't closely follow one existing paper. Applied algorithm implementation and characterization: implement a known algorithm and rigorously characterize its behavior, rather than simply demonstrating that it runs. None of these require inventing a genuinely new algorithm or proving a new theorem.

Reproduction plus extension is often the strongest choice because it gives you a concrete, externally-defined target before you add anything of your own — if your reproduction doesn't track the paper reasonably well, you've caught a methodology problem before building an extension on a shaky foundation. Set this expectation now, honestly: your capstone is not expected to be publishable or novel at a PhD-dissertation level. It's expected to be a small, complete, honestly-reported piece of work demonstrating you can carry a real research question from hypothesis to a defensible written conclusion.
Next lesson gives you the structure for writing your capstone proposal — a short document that forces you to commit to a specific hypothesis, method, and scope before you've sunk any time into code.
